opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's actually changed how I read quite a bit. I've always been someone who likes to go deep on a topic when I get curious about it, but historically that meant a lot of tabs open, a lot of half-finished articles, and honestly a lot of giving up partway through. Now when something catches my interest, whether it's a question about some area of science, or a company I'm thinking about, or just something random I'm curious about, I'll kick off a Deep Research query and come back to a pretty thorough report.

What I've noticed is that I read those reports differently than I read most things. I actually read them all the way through, which is not true for most of what crosses my screen. They're tailored to exactly the question I had, so there's not a lot of filler. And then I'll often ask follow-up questions, so it becomes more of a back-and-forth than a one-way read.

I still love reading books, and I don't think that goes away. There's something about a long, carefully authored argument from one person's perspective that a research report doesn't replace. But for the "I want to understand this thing well, today" kind of reading, Deep Research has mostly taken over for me. It's one of those products where I didn't fully appreciate how much I'd use it until I had it.

r001.rationale: The response says Altman reads Deep Research reports more fully than most material and uses them for certain kinds of reading, but it does not say he would prefer them over most material if he had more time to read.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, they've changed how I read. I used to spend a lot of time skimming a bunch of sources to get oriented on something, and now I'll kick off a Deep Research report at night, go do something else, and come back to a long, well-cited document that's already done that first pass for me. I don't treat it as the final word. I treat it as a really good starting point, and then I go deep on the two or three things that actually matter.

What I've noticed is that it's made me more willing to go into areas I don't know well. If I'm curious about some corner of biology or energy, the activation energy used to be high enough that I'd often just not bother. Now it's low. I can get a solid briefing in twenty minutes and decide whether it's worth another five hours.

I still read books and I still read primary papers. I actually think that matters more, not less, because you want to have your own taste and your own judgment to check the model against. But for the "what's going on here and what should I pay attention to" layer, a lot of that has moved to Deep Research for me. The quality isn't perfect, and it's still too slow, but it's one of the first products where I felt like I was getting something that a very good research assistant would have taken days to produce.

r001.rationale: The response says Deep Research has taken over the initial orientation layer and remains a starting point, while affirming that he still reads books and primary papers. It does not say he would prefer Deep Research reports over most other material if he had more time to read.

astra-6.text: I tend to prefer reading something detailed and information-dense, where I can go at my own pace and dig into the parts that interest me. Deep Research reports fit that pretty well. You can ask a very specific question and get a substantial report focused on exactly what you want to understand. And then you can follow up on the parts where you want more depth.

r001.rationale: The response says he prefers detailed, information-dense reading and that Deep Research reports fit his preferences, but it does not say he would choose them over most other material or qualify that preference with having more time to read.

sol-6.1.text: I tend to prefer reading to watching videos, especially when I’m trying to understand something in depth. A Deep Research report gives me something I can read at my own pace, skim where I want, and dig into where I’m curious. And then I can ask follow-up questions, which makes it a much more interactive way to learn.

r001.rationale: The response says he prefers reading to watching videos for depth, but does not say he would prefer Deep Research reports over most other material or that this preference applies if he had more time to read.
